input.incident_description: A ventilator stopped delivering breaths without triggering its alarm during overnight use in the ICU. The patient went into respiratory arrest and died before staff could intervene. The device was a Class III active life-sustaining device.
A patient required emergency surgical intervention after a hip joint replacement implant loosened and caused significant internal bleeding. The implant is a Class III device.

During surgery, the electrosurgical unit produced an unexpected arc that caused a superficial burn on the patient's skin. The device was a Class IIb active therapeutic device. The burn required minor treatment.

A drug-eluting coronary stent appeared to trigger a severe anaphylactic reaction immediately after implantation. The patient required emergency epinephrine administration and was admitted to the ICU for 48 hours.

An insulin infusion pump malfunctioned and delivered five times the programmed dose. The patient developed severe hypoglycemia requiring emergency glucose administration and overnight ICU admission for monitoring.

A nurse noticed that a disposable syringe plunger was slightly stiff to push during a routine injection. No incorrect dose was delivered, the patient experienced no harm, and the syringe was discarded and replaced with no clinical impact.

A box of surgical gloves was printed with a slightly smaller font size than specified, but all required label information was present, correct, and legible. No device malfunction occurred and there was no patient contact issue.

A digital thermometer displayed a reading 0.1 degrees Celsius off during a routine calibration check in the biomedical engineering workshop. It was flagged and recalibrated before being returned to clinical use; no patient was involved.
A blood pressure cuff's Velcro fastener was slightly worn but still held securely during a routine checkup. The reading was accurate and the patient was unaffected by the minor wear.

A software update for a hospital's non-clinical appointment-scheduling module contained a typo in a button label. The typo had no effect on any clinical function, diagnosis, treatment, or patient data.
A report was filed describing a possible issue with equipment used during a procedure, but no further details about the device or the patient outcome were provided.
A nurse mentioned that something seemed off with a monitor during a shift, but was unsure whether it affected any reading or had any effect on the patient.
There may have been an issue with an infusion device at some point during a shift; it is unclear what, if anything, happened to the patient as a result.
A possible problem was noted with a surgical tool, though no additional information is available about what occurred or who, if anyone, was involved.
Something was reported about a device malfunction, but details about the device type and any patient impact were not recorded at the time.
